title: The Director of the Year's Sleeper Horror Hit Just Said He'd Rather Never Make the Sequel Than Make It Badly
excerpt: Munjya turned a Konkan folk spirit and zero stars into a ₹132 crore phenomenon. Now Aditya Sarpotdar is refusing to greenlight Munjya 2 until the script clears his own bar — even if that takes ten years.
body:
There's a particular kind of confidence it takes to look at a hit and walk away from the obvious paycheck. **Aditya Sarpotdar** has it.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=8X3uF80H5LU</youtube>

Two years ago, almost nobody outside Maharashtra had heard of a Konkan folk spirit called the Munjya — the restless ghost of a boy who dies unmarried between his thread ceremony and his wedding, doomed to haunt peepal trees and chase the things he never got to have. Sarpotdar built a whole film around him, with no star, no franchise scaffolding, and a CGI creature his team spent over a year sculpting from scratch with the VFX house DNEG. **Munjya** opened on June 7, 2024, and then refused to leave — it crossed ₹132 crore worldwide against a ₹30 crore budget and became one of the highest-grossing Hindi films of that year. It also did something rarer: it lodged itself in the culture. People are still talking about it.

So of course everyone wants a sequel. And of course Sarpotdar, the man who could have it greenlit by lunch, is the one slamming the brakes.

> "I get a lot of messages about it and it's good to know people want to watch it. But that's the point. I can't disappoint them with something that's mediocre. I would rather not make it than deliver something that's not up to the standard." — Aditya Sarpotdar, to Variety India

Read that twice, because it cuts against everything the modern franchise machine stands for. In an industry where a ₹100-crore opening weekend is treated as a mandate to fast-track three more chapters, here's a filmmaker treating his own success as a liability he refuses to squander.

And he's not playing coy for negotiating leverage. Asked about timelines, he shrugged them off entirely: "I'm okay with being asked maybe 10 years later, 'Why didn't you make it?' But until I don't feel that my script matches a certain level or a quality and is something totally new and beyond people's expectations, I will not make it."

Ten years. He said ten years. Most directors won't commit to ten *months* of restraint when there's money on the table.

The context makes the stance even bolder. Munjya isn't a standalone — it's the third pillar of the **Maddock Horror Comedy Universe**, producer **Dinesh Vijan**'s sprawling, interconnected gambit modelled openly on the Marvel playbook. The universe began with **Stree** (2018), exploded with **Stree 2** (2024) and its monstrous ₹880-crore haul, and now stretches across a roadmap that runs all the way to a two-part *Mahayudh* finale in 2028. A film officially titled *Maha Munjya* already sits on that calendar, penciled for a December 2027 release. The franchise has its slot ready. The pressure isn't theoretical — it's literally drawn into the studio's release chart.

Which is exactly why Sarpotdar's line in the sand matters. He's the rare cog who's willing to tell the machine to wait.

There's craft behind the caution, too. When Munjya was still in production, Sarpotdar promised that any sequel would feature an "upgraded version" of the spirit — a bigger budget meaning a bigger, eerier, more expressive creature. He's invoked **Kantara** as his lodestar: proof that a story rooted in a hyper-specific regional legend, told with conviction, can travel anywhere. "Munjya gave me confidence that people will like it," he said of that bet paying off. He knows what he caught lightning in. He just isn't willing to bottle a watered-down version of it.

For the diaspora, this is the cinema that actually translates. The Maddock horror-comedies — **Stree**, **Bhediya**, **Munjya**, **Stree 2**, and last Diwali's **Thamma** — have become reliable family-night streaming staples on Amazon Prime Video, the kind of films where the scares are PG enough for the kids and the folklore is a quiet bridge back to grandmothers' stories. A Munjya sequel done right wouldn't just be a hit; it would be the next entry in a canon that's teaching a generation of NRI kids the names of spirits their parents grew up fearing.

Meanwhile, Sarpotdar isn't sitting idle. His next, the supernatural drama **Shakti Shalini**, has wrapped shooting and is deep in post-production — another piece of the same universe, another chance to prove the formula has legs.

The gamble here is counterintuitive and completely his own: the surest way to protect a beloved character is sometimes to refuse to bring him back. Munjya the spirit waited years between his thread ceremony and the wedding he never got. It seems his director is perfectly comfortable making audiences wait, too — for as long as it takes to get him right.
